beats.say: In 912, the Caliphate founded the Madrasat al-Qurʾān in Córdoba, open to any talented youth.
beats.visual: interior of Madrasat al-Qurʾān Córdoba 912 manuscript

beats.say: Among its pupils was Rodrigo Díaz, a Christian noble who mastered Arabic astronomy and geometry.
beats.visual: portrait of Rodrigo Díaz medieval illustration

beats.say: By 958, Rodrigo translated al-Zarqali's astrolabe tables, secretly circulating them among northern courts.
These manuscripts reached the court of Count Fernán González, who taught them to his soldiers.
In 1011, the Christian king Sancho III of Navarre commissioned a fleet using the improved navigation charts.
The fleet's success against Muslim pirates proved the practical power of Andalusian science.
Soon, the secret school's graduates spread across Iberia, embedding Arabic arithmetic in royal treasuries.
beats.visual: Iberian royal treasury accounting records Arabic numerals

beats.say: When the Reconquista intensified, Christian leaders demanded these scholars, turning former rivals into allies.
By 1085, the famed library of Toledo, rescued from the siege, housed the very texts they taught.
Centuries later, this hidden curriculum seeded the European scientific awakening that reshaped the world.
